title: Surveillance and the Cost of Being Watched
text:
Governments and corporations increasingly collect data about citizens' movements, purchases and conversations. Defenders of such surveillance argue that it deters crime and improves public services. Critics reply that the mere possibility of being observed alters behaviour, encouraging people to censor themselves even when they have nothing to hide.

The debate is complicated by the fact that data, once gathered, is rarely confined to its original purpose. Information collected for one stated reason may later be repurposed, sold or breached. Consequently, several legal scholars propose that privacy be treated not as a private preference but as a collective good that protects the conditions for free thought.

questions.text: According to the first paragraph, what do defenders argue surveillance does?
options: Deters crime and improves public services

questions.text: What does the second paragraph say often happens to data collected for one purpose?
options: It is rarely confined to its original purpose

questions.text: What does the passage imply about the effect of being observed?
options: It has no influence on behaviour
It may encourage self-censorship even among innocent people
It makes people more willing to commit crime

questions.text: Why might scholars treat privacy as a collective good?
options: Because it benefits only individuals who have secrets
Because it protects the conditions for free thought across society
Because governments own all personal information
Because it is cheaper to maintain than public services

discourages someone from doing something through fear of consequences
adapted for a use different from the original one
broken into or accessed without authorisation

paragraph_translations: Governos e corporações coletam cada vez mais dados sobre os movimentos, as compras e as conversas dos cidadãos. Os defensores dessa vigilância argumentam que ela dissuade o crime e melhora os serviços públicos. Os críticos respondem que a mera possibilidade de ser observado altera o comportamento, levando as pessoas a se autocensurarem mesmo quando não têm nada a esconder.

O debate se complica pelo fato de que os dados, uma vez coletados, raramente se limitam ao propósito original. Informações reunidas por um motivo declarado podem depois ser reutilizadas, vendidas ou violadas. Consequentemente, vários estudiosos do direito propõem que a privacidade seja tratada não como uma preferência individual, mas como um bem coletivo que protege as condições do pensamento livre.
